utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please bring in the accused. (The accused entered court) Would the Registry please call to order the matter before us for this session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-95-14-T, the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are meeting here today in order to decide on an order for the production of documents. This order was issued by this Chamber. It is dated back to 30th January 1998, which dealt with a request from the Republic of Croatia. It was appealed. So, we come together now to hear Croatia and all of the parties. First I would like to identify each of the parties present. Now, is Croatia present, or rather the leader of the representatives who would be presenting the arguments present here today? If so, please stand so we may identify that person and, of course, I would like to greet them. AMBASSADOR MULJACIC: Hello, Mr President. My name is Mr Muljacic, Ambassador for the Republic of Croatia in the Netherlands. At my side is Mr Casey, who is the legal counsel for the Republic of Croatia, and Mr Rivkin, as a counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Rivkin is which person?

utterances.speaker: MR. RACIC
utterances.text: He is the legal advisor for the Republic of Croatia, and Mr Miljenic, who is the First Secretary for the Croatian Embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, first of all, for expressing yourself in my native language, which is one of the working languages of the Tribunal. Forgive me if I do not pronounce your names correctly. I would like now to turn to the Prosecution, Mr Harman, who will identify himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr President and your Honours, Mr Ambassador, counsel, colleagues. My name is Mark Harman and I will be representing the Prosecutor's Office in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now for the other party, that being the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr President, your Honours. My colleague Mr Hayman and I, Mr Nobilo, will represent the Defence for General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let me now remind you then of the matter for us. The binding order which I had signed with regards to the Republic of Croatia was issued on 30th January. According to this order, Croatia was bound to produce a number of documents to the Prosecutor by 27th February at the latest. This was an application of Rule 108 of the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal. The Republic of Croatia issued a request for the review of this decision on the binding order. I am not going to the details of the reasons for such a request, but I will simply go to the decision of the Appeals Chamber. This was rendered on 26th February 1998, which -- I will read the decision to you. This was the case that was before the Chamber, Judge Riad and Judge Shahabuddeen, for which the Republic of Croatia and the parties should be heard on the issue of the binding orders. Therefore, also decided to stay on the execution of this order which I had asked them to take. So, this was the order that was issued and so for this particular case, I am going to ask for the successive members here, first of all the Republic of Croatia, to take the floor, since this decision by the Appeals Chamber concerns primarily the Republic of Croatia, which has not been heard, then the Prosecution, which was the initial person who made the request. I will also ask for them to issue their own statement. Then lastly, of course, it will be the judges who will put questions to all the parties. Would all the members here from the Republic of Croatia like to take the floor, or how have you organised yourselves? Would you like to speak or how is that to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. RACIC
utterances.text: No, our legal advisor, Mr Rivkin, will be the main orator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr Rivkin, therefore, you have the floor on behalf of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May it please the court, at the outset I wanted to deliver a very short statement that would set forth the way the Republic of Croatia sees the issues here and would be happy to entertain your questions. Our hope is, as a result of this hearing, we would be able to narrow down the request for production of documents in ways that comports better with the relevant decisions of an Appellate Chamber. At the outset, it is important to recall the status of the Republic of Croatia in this case. In that respect, Croat's position is no different from that of any other party. It is not a party before this court, or otherwise connected with the substance of this Prosecution. In fact, Croatia has no stake in the outcome of this stake whatsoever, except that Croatia passionately cares about relevant principles of international law. Croatia is a third party, from whom the Prosecution is seeking to obtain documents or documentary evidence for use at the trial stage. It is right to do so in our view under Article 29(2) of the Tribunal Statute in these circumstances is quite limited. In this regard, it is important to restate briefly what we are dealing with here is a binding order issued under Article 29(2), rather than merely a request for cooperation under Article 29(1). The scope of requests which may be the subject of a binding order under Article 29(2) was articulated by the Appeals Chamber in its original 29th October 1997 judgment. In that judgment, the Appeals Chamber specifically considered "whether binding orders for the production of documents addressed to State can be broad in scope or whether they must instead be specific". The Chamber made clear that the United States-style discovery requests, seeking broad categories of unspecified documents that may or may not contain relevant evidence, are not appropriate for requests or orders for the production of documents under Article 29(2) of the Tribunal's Statute. Instead the Appeals Chamber established a series of threshold requirements that must be met by any Prosecutorial request for documents to be issued to a State in the form of a binding order. These requirements are as follows: (1) the request must "identify specific documents and not broad categories." That is to say, the documents must both be "identified as far as possible and in addition be limited in number". As a general rule, the Appeals Chamber made clear that documents must be identified by title, date and author or other particulars. As a concession to Defence counsel, and as an exception to this general rule, which I just articulated, the Appeals Chamber also stated that if a particular document cannot be identified by title, date and author or other particulars, the party may omit such details so long as it explains why that is the case and nevertheless identifies the "specific documents in question in some appropriate manner". I believe here it is important to note that the Trial Chamber may allow the omission, in our view, of course, of the details of title, date and author only if (1) it is satisfied that the requesting party is acting in good faith, and "has no means of providing those particulars". Moreover, even if the Trial Chamber determines that the details of title, date and author for a particular document may be omitted from the request, the requesting party still must identify specific documents, and not broad categories of documents as the Prosecution has done here. We believe effectively, enough detail must be provided so that the document or documents sought can be identified, i.e., separated from all the other documents that may be in the government archives. Any request that asks for categories of "any and all" documents - as do most of the Prosecutor's request in the order issued on January 30th, on its face, do not meet these requirements set forth by the Appellate Chamber. In this regard, it should also be noted that it is inherently incredible that almost all of the Prosecutor's categorical requests would fall within a narrow exception to the general rule articulated by the Appellate Chamber. In addition, we believe that any request must set out the reasons why the documents are "deemed relevant to the trial". If setting forth these reasons would "jeopardise its prosecutorial or defence strategy", then and only then may a party be excused from stating specific reasons for relevance at trial. It is important to note here that no other reason is sufficient. Moreover, the party must, at the very least, explain the general grounds on which its requests rests. Although some of the categories of documents requested by the Prosecution may conceivably contain documents relevant to the Blaskic trial, it is impossible to make any such determination unless and until the specific documents sought are sufficiently identified by the Prosecution. The Prosecution's request, according to the Appellate Chamber, also cannot be "unduly onerous". Here the Appeals Chamber restated the unqualified injunction that "a party cannot request hundreds of documents". Again, because the Prosecution has asked for categories of documents, and not for specific documents as required by the Appeal Chamber's 29th October decision, it is impossible for us to tell the exact number of documents that might fall into the categories it has demanded. However, most of these categories ask for all documents and records related to certain matters, hence it is very likely that hundreds of documents might be considered to be responsible. Finally, the requested State from which the documents have been requested must be given sufficient time for compliance. It is very important -- and I believe for us to identify our view that it is incorrect to assume that because Croatia has been contesting the Prosecutor's wide-ranging document demands for many months, that it is in position immediately to provide the documents it seeks. Once a request is reduced to a manageable listing of specific documents - as required by the Appeals Chamber judgment, Croatia will seek to comply with that request as expeditiously as possible. Indeed, once such a listing is provided, Croatia then will and must determine whether the specific documents listed exist, where they are located, and who is custody. The documents must be reviewed on an individual basis to determine whether any national security issues (which would have to be independently raised with the Trial Chamber) are presented by the request. I believe that the Trial Chamber should take these considerations into account in establishing the deadline for compliance with whatever list of documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: -- the Trial Chamber should take these considerations into account in establishing a deadline for compliance with whatever revised document request is produced to us out of this hearing. Just a couple of additional points to illustrate our concerns with the current request for documents. The Prosecutor's current request is incorporated into the January 30 order. In our view, it is inconsistent with the requirements of October 29 Appeals Chamber decision. Although the Prosecution has made some cosmetic changes to the listing of documents contained in the subpoena duces tecum quashed by the Appeals Chamber, the order of January 30 remains in substance the same listing. For example, this listing still utilises the form of US-style discovery requests seeking "any and all records, documents, orders and reports" rather than the specific listing of identified materials required by the Appeals Chamber decision. As an example, we wish to draw the Chamber's attention to category 7A of the confidential and ex parte annex to the Chamber's January 30 order. This request asks, among other things, for: "All Croatian government, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior documents, records, reports and orders reflecting the presence and deployment locations of HV military and police units from May 1992 to January 1994, including, but not limited to the HV units described in paragraph VII(B) below." It is very interesting that the same request appeared in the original subpoena duces tecum as formulated as follows: "All Croatian government, Ministry of Defence documents, records, reports and orders reflecting the presence of HV military personnel and their activities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from November 1991 to 1st July 1994, including, but not limited to the following HV military units." Ironically the latter request is, in fact, broader than the original request quashed by the Appeals Chamber. Under that request, any Croatian Ministry of Defence or Ministry of Interior documents reflecting the deployment of the Croatian military or police, anywhere, is called for -- this could include anything from classified documents, detailing Croatia's armed services deployments to records of parking tickets issued by the police in Zagreb, since those records would indeed: "Reflect the presence and deployment locations of ... police units from May 1992 to January 1994." It would be difficult for us to contrive a better example of a classic fishing expedition of the sort the Appeals Chamber foreclosed in its October 29 decision. A similar decision can be found in category VII of the January 30 annex. That category calls for: "All Croatian government documents and records, including those of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Interior, which reflect the death, wounding or injury to HV military, policy, police and intelligence personnel which occurred in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1 January 1993 to 1 January 1994." This request also closely tracks category 12 of the original subpoena duces tecum, which demanded: "All Croatian government Ministry of Defence documents and records reflecting the death, wounding or injury to HV military personnel which occurred in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1 January 1993 to 1 January 1994." Again, the January 30 request actually is broader than the original one and, leaving aside the obvious questions of relevance -- since the fighting which is the subject of this Prosecution did not begin until March 1993, and took place in the Lasva Valley as opposed to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- this request would literally cover material from casualty reports prepared by the Ministry of Defence to individual medical records, to casual mentions in entirely unrelated documents of injuries. This is, of course, assuming that there were HV units somewhere in Bosnia during the requested time period. These requests and most of the others represented in the January 30 annex are, in fact, the very type of US discovery request forbidden by the Appeals Chamber. They are a classic fishing expedition -- the Prosecution clearly does not know what materials it needs for this trial. The Prosecution is still using this as a means of foraging through Croatia's government documents to determine whether there may be some evidence that might support this case. This activity is simply not supported by the Tribunal's Statute or Rules and was, with great specificity and particularity, rejected by the Appeals Chamber's October 29 decision. We also believe that it is entirely possible for the Prosecution to meet the requirements of the Appeals Chamber judgment. It is not the case where they have to choose between complying with it and meeting their -- whatever prosecutorial imperatives they might have. For example, if the purpose of a Prosecution's requested category VII is to obtain official figures on casualties that may have been suffered by Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- assuming for these purposes that HV forces might have been present in that country -- and the Prosecution genuinely cannot determine the title, date and author of the document it seeks, it may omit these details. The Prosecution must nevertheless frame its request so that the individual document or documents it seeks can be identified, so that its relevance and potential privilege status asserted and then produced. The Prosecution, again, cannot, consistent with the Appeal Chamber's order, merely demand any and all documents that might have something to do with the matter it has in mind. This puts Croatia in an impossible position of itself trying to guess what the Prosecution wants, and of never being able to satisfy demands. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Harman, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr President. First off, Mr President, we believe that the subpoena that was issued by this Trial Chamber meets the standards that were articulated in the appeals court judgment. Let me now point to the arguments that have been raised by counsel. First, there are principally three arguments, Mr President: that the present order seeks broad categories of documents; the second argument is that the documents sought in the binding order are not relevant; thirdly, the compliance with the document that has been served upon Croatia is unduly burdensome. Let me, first, start with their argument on relevance and their contention that the documents that are sought have no proven relevance to this case. As Mr Rivkin said, Mr President, they are not a party to this case; they have not sat through this trial since 24th June 1997 to know what is relevant and what is not relevant to this case. I would point out to your Honours paragraph 32 of the appeals court decision that says the issue of relevance is not up to Croatia to decide. As the Trial Chamber says in the second complete paragraph in paragraph 32, that it is for the appropriate judge or Trial Chamber: "To make a preliminary assessment of whether the requested items appear relevant and admissible and are identified with sufficient specificity." So, Mr President, first and foremost, the issue of relevance, since your Honours have sat on this trial every day, is a matter for you to determine, not for Croatia to determine. In the appeals judgment that rejected Croatia's contention that the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia could not issue any order to Croatia, the judgment states in paragraph 30 -- and I quote -- first of all, it recognised, Mr President, that Croatia was one of the belligerent states in the conflict. It is quoted in paragraph 30, and I quote the first paragraph: "The former belligerent parties, they are more likely to hold important evidence needed by the International Tribunal." That is a recognition, Mr President, that they have evidence, that they possess it and that that evidence is needed by this Tribunal and, in particular, Mr President, your order reflects that the evidence that has been articulated and described in the binding order issued to Croatia is, in fact, needed. I will be very, very glad in a few minutes to provide additional articulation as to what the relevance of each of these requests has been. Now, Mr President, furthermore, I refer the court to paragraph 65 of the judgment. In paragraph 65, the Appeals Chamber stated, and I quote: "It is therefore evident that military documents or other evidentiary material connected with military operations may be of critical importance." Now, Mr President, the court has asked, and one of the requirements that is articulated in the Appeals Chamber judgment is that the documents that have been requested are relevant. I will be very pleased to, first of all, refer the court to the pleading that was written, that was filed and articulated, the relevance of each of the categories. I am prepared, Mr President, for the purposes of the record, to go through each of the items and articulate the relevance so that the record is complete. If the court wants me to do so, I can do that now. If the court wants me to file something with the court at a later time to make it part of the record, I can do so. I am at your disposal, Mr President. I am prepared to articulate, in respect of each of the requests, the relevance insofar as it does not reveal the Prosecution strategy and in some parts of this, Mr President, I would ask, in describing the relevance, that I be permitted to go in camera with the Trial Chamber to describe that. Whether or not an in camera proceeding is appropriate, certainly the second part of paragraph 32 states that: "If, essentially the request articulating the relevance might jeopardise the prosecutorial strategy, it may say so." I am saying so at this point, that some of these requests may jeopardise the Prosecution strategy. I am prepared to tell the Trial Chamber the relevance, but absent Croatia and absent my colleagues who are sitting at the bench with me today. I am at your disposal, Mr President, in respect of articulating with specificity the relevance of each of these requirements. If the court wishes me to do so, I will start. In respect, Mr President, of request in the binding order number 1A, B and C, there are three parts of that, those are relevant to prove the international armed conflict component of the grave breaches charges of the indictment, which are counts 5, 8, 11, 15, 17 and 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which order are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: I am talking about your order, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the annex which was attached to the order of 30th January; is that right? We are talking about the same thing, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about item 1A, B and C, and the relevance, Mr President, of those items is to establish the international armed conflict component of the conflict. That is relevant to all grave breach counts of the indictment. Item D, Mr President, is relevant to show aspects relating to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan which the court has heard evidence about, and evidence about any ultimatum that had been issued by the HVO by 15th April 1993. Paragraph 1E is relevant to paragraphs 6.6, 6.7 and 7 of the indictment. In respect, Mr President, of the second item of the annex, that is the request that reflects the military service of four individuals in the Croatian Army. They have been identified with specificity, we believe, Mr President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the proper conduct of this hearing, at this point you are arguing what you wanted to argue in ex parte? Is that what you are doing here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Some of these items, I can articulate without articulating them ex parte. Some of them I can articulate publicly. I am prepared to articulate some; however the court wishes to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, continue. What I had understood was that as regards the entire argument relating to relevance, and specificity of documents, that you were saying that we were prepared to demonstrate the relevance but in a subsequent private session, during which you would show, through documents, what the relevance was. That is what I had understood. Now when I listen to you, it seems you are already arguing the relevance. The judges do not really care, but we would like to understand what it is you prefer to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Very frankly, I prefer arguing this part of the argument in camera, in private. Not having heard a response from your Honour, I assumed you wanted me to proceed in public, I was prepared to do that in some respects, but I prefer doing it in private, as I had with my initial filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you talking about an ex parte hearing or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: "Yes" to what? I asked you whether or not you wanted a closed session or an ex parte session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: An ex parte session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see, very well. Let me consult with my colleagues. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Mr President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: May Croatia be heard very briefly on this issue before you render your decision, on the issue of closed hearing versus ex parte hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I will, of course, give you the floor, but do not forget we must also give the floor to the Defence. I am going to give the floor once again to the Prosecution, but also ask them that they not deal with the issue of relevance. Do you have other observations you would like to make on other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do not go to demonstrating the criteria that the Appeals Chamber has used in dealing with this request. Do you have other observations you would like to make in a general manner dealing with the order that you can make now? Then we will give the floor for observations from Mr Hayman, then we will end with Croatia. Then the judges will decide whether they feel that an ex parte hearing is necessary to deal with the criteria used by the Appeals Chamber or the documents that have been requested. Mr Harman, please go on with your general observations in addition to what you have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, I will say no more at this point in respect of relevancy. The next argument Croatia has raised is the argument that the Prosecutor is absolutely prohibited from requesting categories of documents. Now, the Appeals Court decision, Mr President, in paragraph 32, made a qualified prohibition. It essentially said, Mr President, said that where the Prosecutor cannot identify with specificity certain types of documents it requests, it should be relieved of the requirement to make that kind of specific identification. Furthermore, the Appellate Chamber said, and I quote: "The Trial Chamber may consider it appropriate, in view of the spirit of the Statute and the need to ensure a fair trial, to Rule 89(b) and (d) to allow the omission of those details if it is satisfied that the party requesting the order, acting bona fide, has no means of providing those details." Therein, Mr President and your Honours, is the dilemma faced by the Prosecutor, and I am sure this argument Croatia understands: we do not have access to the Ministry of Defence documents; we do not have access to communications between Croatian military leaders, political leaders and military leaders to HVO political and military leaders. It is absolutely impossible for the Prosecutor's Office to identify with specificity the documents that it seeks. So, the approach taken by the Prosecutor's Office with this binding order has been to make it as unonerous as possible on Croatia as we can. We have attempted, through this binding order, to narrow down, as much as possible, the categories so as to lessen the burden on Croatia, which has had 15 months, to find documents that are related to the request. Now, Mr President, you must have to ask yourselves, as I asked myself: would it be prudent of the Prosecutor's Office to ask Croatia for some of the relevant documents; leaving the discretion to Croatia to decide what relevant evidence will be produced to the Prosecutor's Office and to the Chamber, because, Mr President, precisely because we have been unable to identify with specificity the documents that we seek, having attempted in good faith to narrow down the requests as much as possible, and given Croatia's utter failure and unwillingness to provide the requested documents for over 15 months, it would be foolish of the Prosecutor's Office to substitute the word "some" for the word "all" documents, thereby giving Croatia the right to select what relevant evidence should come before this Trial Chamber. Now, Mr President, if you wish I will -- I take serious issue with Croatia's characterisation that the documents that are requested are not precisely and specifically identified. If you will bear with me for just a moment, Mr President. The documents that are found in paragraph 1 of the binding order are requests which identify two sources of documents and requests five different categories of documents. So, we are limiting the category, the type of document from two sources. Mr President, the second requested item requests records reflecting military service of four individuals in the Croatian Army. Every military that I am aware of keeps those kind of records, Mr President. They keep personnel files. To suggest that it is onerous to obtain the personnel files of four individuals who are in the Croatian military is preposterous. The third requested item, Mr President, is records that reflect remuneration by Croatia to those four individuals. Again, Mr President, every military service keeps those kinds of records. To suggest that it is onerous on Croatia to find pay records for four individuals, for a limited period of time, is preposterous. Mr President, the fourth item that has been requested are documents and reports about specific attacks, limited in time and location, that were prepared by or for then Colonel Blaskic or the HVO or the HZB authorities or prepared by or for a man by the name of Siskovic and his representatives, including a very specific document that was found in attachment B. That pretty much narrows the burden on Croatia to locate those documents. The particular report that was found in attachment B, Mr President, is an order purportedly signed by then Colonel Blaskic requesting an investigation and requesting that the SIS perform that investigation and inquiry. So, Mr President, the fourth item has been narrowed down in terms of geographic location, in terms of time and specifically in terms of people for whom these reports were prepared. In terms of the fifth item, Mr President, we have narrowed that request down considerably. It is a request reflecting -- requesting the names of persons who were prosecuted and disciplined for the crimes that took place in the village of Ahmici and other villages in the Lasva Valley in April 1993; again, limited in number, Mr President, and limited in scope. The fourth request, which is records reflecting the provision of military weapons, ammunition, communications equipment and personnel by Croatia to the HVO in Herceg-Bosna between May 1992 and January of 1994, narrows the request in terms of time, furthermore, Mr President, it is narrower than the previous request, because the previous request had requested medical and logistical supplies. So we have tried to narrow that down further. The sixth -- I am sorry, Mr President. The seventh item that has been requested is an item that was commented on by counsel and perhaps, on rereading that, I take his point. He has suggested that it might result in the Prosecutor's Office receiving traffic tickets from Zagreb. I fear that I might just be on the receiving end of traffic tickets from Zagreb, so I am prepared to try to attempt to narrow that down even further. The second part of item 7, I would like to point out there is an error in that and I would like to narrow it further. Under 7B it requests documents since "November 1991"; that is an error, it should be "November of 1992". This request furthermore, Mr President, 7B, narrows the request to combat activities against the Armija, the Bosnian Muslim Army, in that timeframe -- not to the Serbs, so it is very specific as to the location and the combatants. The eighth item, Mr President, are records reflecting casualties, death and wounding and injury of Croatian military police, military and intelligence personnel. I have an exhibit I will present the court at the conclusion of this presentation, but these are the kind of items, Mr President, that most militaries keep. They keep them because they have to pay benefits to injured and dead soldiers and the dependents of those soldiers. The items articulated in item 9, Mr President, Croatia has conceded that that, in one of its pleadings, approximates the specificity that it thinks is appropriate. Items 10, Mr President, and 11, are very specific requests. It requests visitor logs, those kind of items traditionally kept by members of State. It requests minutes and reports of those meetings and if the court would permit me, Mr President, I would like to add -- I would like to somewhat broaden the request in this particular -- I would ask for all tape recordings of those meetings to be included in the item number 10. Number 11, Mr President, is the same. Now, Mr President, I would like to submit to the court that the kind of record that Croatia has struggled so valiantly to locate. It relates to item number 7 and it is -- I need to explain these documents. I have a set for counsel, I have a set for the representatives from Croatia and for your Honours. With the assistance of the usher, if these could be distributed and marked, I will then explain to the court what these documents are. Perhaps this can shed some light and give some guidance to Croatia in terms of the type of documents that we are seeking to locate. (Handed). Mr President, I have just received these documents. They are not translated into French. They are translated into English. There are three documents. The first is a report of a death. This is the report of a death of an individual whose name appears on the right-hand side of the full block. It indicates that this death occurred -- this death was of a member of the 145th Brigade of the Croatian Army, the second. It is a death certificate, Mr President, that has been sent to the Registry in Zagreb. The second document, Mr President, is a report from Herceg-Bosna from Mostar, describing the circumstances of the death of this particular individual. This says that he was killed in combat against Muslim armed forces at a particular location on a particular date. The third document, Mr President, is a document that indicates that the individual who was killed was, in fact, a member of the Croatian Army. It is the funeral notice. Mr President, these documents -- so it is perfectly clear -- later on these -- these documents are submitted to your Honour as illustrative only. They are to illustrate for the court, for Croatia's sake, the type of documents that we are seeking. I am not suggesting they are exclusively the kind of documents that the Croatian military possesses, but they may possess this kind of a document. Mr President, later on, for the record, so it is perfectly clear, it appears that this individual was killed by a member of the HVO and not by a member of -- in combat with the Muslim forces, from the information that I have. Furthermore, Mr President, it appears from the information that is available to me, that he was a Croatian soldier who was sent to the southern front and he was, at the time of his death, wearing an HVO patch. There is litigation that was started in Croatia in respect of his death. That litigation was transferred to the court in Mostar. At this point, Mr President, that is the information I know about these particular documents. Mr President, my point is simply this: militaries keep records of people who get killed in the service of their country. Croatia, I am sure, Mr President, is no exception. In fact, Mr President, this man, from the information I know, was made later, posthumously, an honorary captain of the Croatian Army. I present these documents, Mr President, only as evidence and as illustrations of the kind of documents that perhaps will clarify the type of documents that I am seeking and lessen Croatia's burden. The third argument of Croatia is that complying with the order that is before -- that your Honours' have issued to Croatia is unduly burdensome. So the record is perfectly clear, Mr President. The initial subpoena duces tecum which was contested as a matter of principle by Croatia and which I accept was issued to Croatia on 15th January 1997. In the hearing that occurred before Judge McDonald on 19th February, the subpoena duces tecum was suspended by Judge McDonald on the representation of Ambassador Salih that they objected to the form of the request. On 19th February 1997, the Prosecutor's Office served upon Croatia, and Croatia accepted, a formal request for assistance. Those documents Mr President, I filed with the court. Now, Mr President, Croatia has never contested the request for assistance. In fact, shortly after 19th February, Ambassador Salih wrote to the Prosecutor's Office informing the Prosecutor's Office that a meeting would take place in Croatia on 26th February 1997. He expected that certain documents, pursuant to the request for assistance, would be provided to the Prosecutor's Office. The Prosecutor's Office sent representatives to Croatia. We received no documents in response to the request for assistance. We were assured at that meeting, Mr President, that Croatia was looking for and attempting to locate documents that were responsive to the request for assistance. Subsequently, the Prosecutor's Office received a report back from the Republic of Croatia that, in respect of some of the earlier documents, they did not have any. Furthermore, Mr President, they reported back that some of our requests were not relevant. Again, Mr President, the issue of relevance is for the Chamber to decide, not for Croatia to decide. One can hardly say, Mr President, with a straight face, that in the past 15 months that Croatia has had since it received the subpoena duces tecum and the 14 months since they received the Prosecutor's response for assistance, that they have cooperated in good faith with the Prosecutor's Office in attempting to find documents showing that it was -- it, Croatia, was involved in an international armed conflict. Indeed, very frankly, Mr President, the relevance of many of these documents would establish just that fact. It is clearly not in Croatia's perceived international interest to admit to the -- submit evidence that it participated in a war against Bosnia. So, Mr President, our efforts to -- our cooperative efforts with Croatia over the past 15 months have yielded extremely little in terms of evidence that has been sought in this particular binding order. I can say, Mr President, that I received a stack of documents, about an inch. It contained gasoline receipts and receipts for sheriffs' badges and the like. In terms of evidence that has been sought and that may appear to be similar to the request for assistance, that may appear to be similar to the initial subpoena, that request and those efforts on the cooperative side by Croatia have yielded virtually nothing. So, I think, Mr President, that the request for a binding order does, in fact, comply with the parameters set forth by the Appeals Chamber judgment. I would ask, Mr President, given the exegeses of trial, which is something that is recognised in the trial itself, that we proceed on full compliance with the order, lest, Mr President, we find ourselves in a position where the Prosecutor will rest its case without having the benefit of its right under a binding order and its expectation that Croatia will comply in good faith. I do not want to delay this trial, Mr President, but the Prosecutor's Office does insist that it have the benefit of evidence that is in the possession and exclusive control of Croatia. I think it is necessary so the court will have a complete and full picture of the events that are now before it and which your Honours are asked to judge. Those, Mr President, save my remarks on the issue of relevance, are all I have to say. Thank you, Mr President, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like now to hear the other party in this case. Is it Mr Hayman who will be speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr President and your Honours. First, let me say I take the Prosecutor's final words as a very ominous statement, that they may seek to delay the trial, depending on their success in trying to obtain records from one entity or another. I would think it is incumbent on the Prosecutor to get his evidence before he indicts the accused. There is nothing wrong with trying to get more evidence, but we would strongly object -- and will object -- to any attempt to delay the trial on the grounds that the Prosecutor did not have enough evidence and does not have enough evidence to proceed against General Blaskic, given that he was indicted in November of 1995 and has been in custody for two years as of this month. With respect to the issues being discussed here today, we have very little to say, the Defence. We have said before the Appellate Chamber that, in general, our position is the Defence must have the same powers as the Prosecutor with respect to access to proof. In that sense, we reiterate same access and same power means; whatever procedures are imposed on one party, the other should be subject to. There should be the same standard, the same burden, et cetera. We have not seen the application filed in respect of the current request. We have not seen a proposed order, if there is one; hence, we, the Defence, were not in a position to comment on those specific, even if we were asked, and we doubt it is appropriate for us to comment in any event. With respect to the ex parte question, we take the view generally that a party should be able to request ex parte orders from the Trial Chamber to other entities to appear for testimony or for the production of documents. We understand we are only here in this matter for the reason that the Prosecutor choose at a certain point in his applications to file public applications and, indeed, I believe that a press statement was issued. Thus, his right to ex parte proceedings in some measure were waived as a result of those actions. Nonetheless, we do not seek to comment on his specific request other than to say the same standards and procedures should apply to all parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsellor Hayman. Mr Fourmy reminds me -- and he is completely correct in saying so -- that the annex in the request submitted by the Prosecutor was, indeed, confidential and that the order had been made public, as all orders are made public. Of course, there are some exceptions, but, of course, that the annex has remained under seal of confidentiality. Let us be very clear on that particular issue. Now, with regards to Croatia, I think you would like also to respond; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In fact, if -- may it please the court, we would like to proceed in the following fashion: I would have a couple of very brief remarks and I would have a colleague of mine, Mr Casey, respond on behalf of Croatia to several specific observations about various of categories documents that were described by the Prosecution. My brief remarks are as follows: we understand the need, in a number of circumstances, for ex parte hearings. We would feel very strongly that, to the greatest extent possible, we would prefer a closed hearing on the issue of relevance and specificity because, to so state one key point here, if all those issues are discussed in an ex parte hearing, we would have no opportunity -- the State of Croatia would have no opportunity to benefit from the specific provisions set forth in the two orders of the Appellate Chamber. I would also like to point out in a way -- I do not want to put a word in the mouth of my colleague on the Prosecution side, but it appears that the Prosecution has admitted that it can go, at least, part of the way and deal with some relevancy and specificity issues, especially specificity issues, not in an ex parte context. What I would urge your Honours to do is to take advantage of it, offer it -- it does not have to be, as we see it, with all due respect, an overall proposition. What I am trying to say, in our view we do not have to choose between a hearing where all of the relevancy and specificity issues are aired which may trouble the Prosecution, or have an ex parte hearing where none of those issues are articulated in our presence; there can be something in between. As I said, it appears to me from listening to the Prosecution that they are prepared to proceed in this fashion. If I may turn things over to my colleague, Mr Casey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I wanted to respond briefly to a couple of the points made by the Prosecution, if I may. First of all, I wanted to point out that if you read carefully paragraph 32 of the Appellate Chamber's October 29th decision, it does not relieve the Prosecution of its obligation to specify exactly which documents it wants and not ask for broad categories. All the Appellate Chamber said was that if the Prosecution or a party cannot identify a document by title, date, author of documents or other particulars of that sort, then the party may be allowed to omit such details, provided it explains the reasons therefore and, quoting: "Should still be required to identify the specific documents in some appropriate manner." We would contend that that appropriate manner may not be by name and date, but by description. In that regard, your Honour, I think we have actually made substantial progress this afternoon. We have seen, for example, beginning with category 2, which, if you look at annex -- if you look at the secret annex, asks for records which: "Reflect service in the HV military police and intelligence services of the following individuals." Well, "records", of course, is not defined and, in fact, could be read to request any piece of paper in the possession of the Croatian Government that refers to these gentlemen. I now understand that what the Prosecution wants is their personnel files. Well, if such personnel files do exist, we can now go and find them and perhaps be in a position to actually produce them, assuming there are no other privileges that would have to be raised independently with the Trial Chamber. The same is true for category 3, which, as it was propounded, requests records which reflect remuneration by Croatia to certain individuals. Again, "records" is unclear. Now we understand that what they are looking for is payroll stubs, records. Again, that can be identified and if it exists, perhaps can be turned over. Category number 8, I think was also one that the Prosecution mentioned this afternoon, which, as propounded, asks for all Croatian Government documents and records, including those in the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior which reflect the death or wounding or injury of HV military police and intelligence personnel in Bosnia from January 1993 to January 1994. Again, that could refer to anything in the Government's records, be it newspaper articles or reports of death which the Prosecution has produced. Again, if what the Prosecution wants is reports of death, then that is something that we can go back and see if they exist for those periods of time and, perhaps, produce. That is something that you can understand what they are looking for and you can then attempt to produce it. I would suggest, your Honour, that the Prosecution should be required for each of these categories, where they have not already done so, to identify with that kind of specificity what it is they are looking for and then we will be in a position to meet the court's order. Finally, I wanted to say one remark regarding the issue raised by the Prosecution on the request for assistance. Again, I think we have to keep in mind that we are dealing here with a separate animal. A request for assistance can, indeed, be broad. It is something that is a matter of cooperation between the Prosecutor's Office and the State. All the State is required to do is basically use its best efforts to try to comply. An order is very, very different. An order, as the Appellate Chamber indicated, could result, if Croatia does not satisfy the order, in a report to the UN Security Council, suggesting that Croatia is in violation of its international obligations, which is a very serious matter. I think, consequently, orders must be much more specific and it must be much more definite so that the Government can actually determine what it needs to do to comply. I would submit, under the current order for most of these categories, it simply cannot do that. Your Honour, if you have any questions, I would be happy to answer, otherwise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). The Chamber would like to issue the following order. We are going to take a 20-minute recess. Then we are going to resume with a closed session, solely with the presence of Croatia and the Prosecution. The Defence then will not be able to give its observations at that time. At the closing of this closed session, which will enable us to determine the substance of the future order that this Chamber will be making, if, within this time period, within this closed session -- the Prosecutor said he was not completely opposed to the idea of an open session. If we find, during this ex parte session that there are reasons to have another ex parte hearing then, we then decide on that matter at that time. From 20 minutes or 15 minutes from now we are going to have a closed session solely between Croatia and the Prosecution. We now stand adjourned and will begin once again at 5.05 pm.
